proposals.relationship: As Dagbovie recounts, Du Bois valued Woodson’s factual research but criticized his church history for failing to interpret the inner meanings of Black religious experience.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Dagbovie’s 2012 study, printed17–18 and note29, reconstructs Du Bois’s 1922 review. The acknowledgment of useful fact-finding and the earlier praise for Woodson’s education study remain alongside the methodological objection. Du Bois’s original Freeman review,4October1922,92–93, and Aptheker’s 1977 reprint,67–68, were not independently read. Woodson’s full church history remains unread; this is an attributed judgment, not an editorial finding of inadequacy.
primary_locators: Dagbovie2012, printed17–18 (PDF27–28 zero-based), paragraph beginning Based on his background through the end of the Du Bois church-review discussion; note29.

proposals.relationship: Du Bois recommends the first edition of Woodson’s The Negro in Our History as a resource for Black historical education.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1935 essay, printed333, expressly recommends the first edition alongside Brawley and the jointly credited Cromwell, Turner and Dykes reader, and also recommends Negro History Week. This records a particular endorsed teaching resource, not a formative influence or approval of all editions. Du Bois distinguishes education from a universal prescription for separate or mixed schools at335. The full Woodson textbook and its edition history were not read.
primary_locators: The Journal of Negro Education4(3),July1935,333, paragraph beginning What I have in mind;335 concluding paragraph. NHC scan PDF pages7,9 (one-based, including cover).

proposals.relationship: Higginbotham recalls that her father’s devotion to Woodson’s historical mission led her into history, a commitment she later deepened through reading Woodson.
proposals.evidence_note: Own oral-history testimony,16June2011, transcribed by Ashley Robertson in the2012 NPS study, printed185 and188. Albert N. D. Brooks is the essential intermediary; this does not make Woodson her personal academic supervisor. Higginbotham also identifies insufficient attention to African American women in the earlier scholars’ groundwork at188; admiration does not erase that qualification. Her father’s recollections, her childhood visits and her later reading remain distinct. Only selected transcript passages were read; no interview recording or full monograph reading is claimed.
primary_locators: AppendixA, interview heading/date and first substantive response, printed185; continuation at188 from childhood Black-history education through her father’s lens and The Mis-Education.
